title: Press a key
subtitle: From PS/2 scancode to the byte your shell read() returns
what_you_see: You type in ash, nano, or vi. Characters echo on the virtual console. Nothing suggests a dozen kernel layers — but every key crosses hardware, interrupts, input, TTY, and a blocking read in userspace.
why_it_matters: Typing is where an OS starts to feel real. One key has to reach the keyboard controller, the interrupt, the input layer, the TTY, and a blocked read — without losing or duplicating the scancode.

steps.label: PS/2 keyboard
steps.what_ir0_does: The i8042 controller latches a scancode in its output buffer. QEMU (or hardware) presents port 0x60/0x64 to the guest.
steps.why_it_matters: Every key begins as electrical signaling, not ASCII.

steps.label: IRQ1
steps.what_ir0_does: The PS/2 controller raises IRQ1. IR0 reads status and data together so the interrupt handler and any poll path never consume the same scancode twice.
steps.why_it_matters: Duplicate keys and lost keys usually trace to this race, not “bad echo logic.”

steps.label: IR0 input layer
steps.what_ir0_does: Set-1 scancode translation produces key events. The input backend can mirror events to `/dev/events0` while the console path consumes characters for the TTY.
steps.why_it_matters: Graphics clients and shells share one keyboard without forking driver code per consumer.

steps.label: /dev/events0
steps.what_ir0_does: evdev-style read path for programs that want structured events (Doom, X). Separate from the TTY byte stream.
steps.why_it_matters: Doom and X need this device to behave like Linux. The shell does not — it reads bytes from the TTY.

steps.label: TTY line discipline
steps.what_ir0_does: Canonical mode, echo, backspace, and sleep when the line buffer is empty. Blocked readers sit on a wait queue until IRQ input wakes them.
steps.why_it_matters: This is why Ctrl+C and line editing feel like Unix.

steps.label: read(0, …)
steps.what_ir0_does: musl issues read on stdin fd 0. Syscall layer routes to the TTY backend; may block until keyboard_feed_scancode → stdin_wake_check runs.
steps.why_it_matters: The boundary between “driver woke me” and “libc returned a char” is the whole OS lesson.

steps.label: ash / nano / vi
steps.what_ir0_does: The program receives bytes and renders them. Job control and line editing are entirely userspace — the kernel only guarantees faithful byte delivery.
steps.why_it_matters: Separation of concerns: kernel transport, userspace policy.
